newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung chides HK Democrats for spreading gloom abroad.
newsitem.headline: Tung chides HK Democrats for spreading gloom abroad.

text.p: Hong Kong leader-in-waiting Tung Chee-hwa on Thursday accused the territory's Democratic Party of spreading gloom overseas about the future of Hong Kong under Chinese rule.

"Recently, some well-known people, including the Democratic Party, have blackened the reputation of Hong Kong overseas... giving the impression that Hong Kong is collapsing," Tung told a news conference.
"This, I feel, is not very good," said Tung, a shipping magnate appointed leader-in-waiting in December, as he arrived at offices that will be his base during the final months of British rule.
Tung said the Democratic Pary was doing a disservice to Hong Kong and its 6.3 million people, who will come under Chinese sovereignty from midnight on June 30.

"We may have different views on the pace of democracy but we can discuss it... But we should discuss this in Hong Kong," he said. "Is there the need to go abroad to blacken the name of Hong Kong? Is there the need for foreigners to come to Hong Kong and tell us, the Hong Kong people, what to do in the future?
"Why can't we be the master of our own destiny and fate?"
The Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, grew out of the shock that gripped Hong Kong in the aftermath of the 1989 Tiananmen Square anti-democracy crackdown in Beijing.
China has branded the party's leaders as subversives and sidelined them from the committees and caucuses responsible for shaping the future of Hong Kong after the 1997 handover.

Party leader Martin Lee has been visiting Europe this month to express concerns that China is set to roll back Hong Kong's freedoms after the handover, despite Beijing's promises to maintain the territory's freedoms and capitalist way of life for 50 years.
Lee has urged the European Union to oppose China's plan to dilute human rights laws in Hong Kong and dismantle its elected legislature upon the handover.
China insists the changes are merely technical and will not curtail freedoms in Hong Kong.
